answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, NLSY79, n=12,686): YES — higher time preference (greater present-orientation) is associated with higher BMI in later adulthood.

Operationalization. Time preference is not directly measured in this file; I proxy it with the only explicit savings-behavior wave (1989), the NLSY variable "Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989" (1=PUT MORE IN, 2=TOOK MORE OUT, 3=NO CHANGE, 4=NO SAVINGS), corroborated by "Net amount put into savings, 1989" and "Net amount taken out of savings, 1989". Putting money INTO savings = delaying gratification = LOW time preference; taking money OUT of savings or having NO savings = present-oriented = HIGH time preference. Outcome BMI at 1992 (measured AFTER the 1989 exposure) is computed from "Weight of respondent, 1992" and adult height ("Height of respondent, 1985", fallback "Height of respondent, 1981"); I validated two data facts: Height 1981 is coded feet*100+inches (507 = 5'7" = 67 in) and Weight values are empirically in POUNDS despite the codebook's "kilograms" label (BMI = 703*lb/in^2; treating raw values as kg gives implausible median BMI ~49).

Primary confounder-adjusted OLS (n=3,311 complete cases; SEs clustered by Sample ID; controls = age 1989, sex, race/ethnicity, family size, mother's/father's education, own education (highest grade 1979), ASVAB composite, family income 1979/1985/1989, family net wealth 1985/1990, incarcerated-ever (sentenced)):
- HEADLINE binary (high TP = took money out OR no savings): +0.54 BMI units (95% CI 0.15–0.94; p=0.007).
- Categorical vs put-money-in reference: TOOK MONEY OUT +0.50 [0.16, 0.84; p=0.004]; NO CHANGE +0.32 [-0.25, 0.89; ns]; NO SAVINGS +0.96 [0.31, 1.61; p=0.004] — a monotone present-orientation gradient matching the unadjusted BMI means (put-in 25.4 < took-out 26.2 ≈ unchanged 26.2 < no-savings 26.7). No result contradicts this gradient.

Robustness: R1 savers-vs-drawers +0.51 [0.11, 0.91]; R2 log(net savings) -0.030/log-unit (more saving -> LOWER BMI, p=0.001, mirror image); R3 same-wave BMI 1989 +0.42 [-0.02, 0.85; p=0.059]; R4 BMI change 1989→1992 -0.06 [ns] (higher TP raises BMI LEVELS but not 1989-92 growth); R5 implausible-BMI exclusion unchanged; R6 median-imputed covariates (n=8,503): took-out +0.43 [0.22, 0.63], no-savings +0.52 [0.22, 0.82], both p<0.001; R7 sex subgroups: women +0.82 [0.11, 1.53; p=0.024], men +0.27 [-0.07, 0.61; ns] (effect concentrated in women); R8 adding father's occupation-at-14 +0.55 [0.16, 0.93]; R9 wealth-accumulation 1985→1996 proxy alone -0.005 [ns] (alternate proxy does NOT replicate); R10 BMI 1981 (measured BEFORE the 1989 exposure) +0.23 [-0.01, 0.46; p=0.055] (a pre-existing gradient — flagging a stable-trait/selection component).

Conclusion: increased time preference, proxied by drawing down or not holding savings in 1989, predicts moderately higher BMI by 1992 after comprehensive confounder control (~+0.5–0.6 BMI units, ≈0.1 SD, roughly 3–4 lb for an average-height adult). Interpretation is observational: "leads to" reflects temporal precedence (1989→1992), not proven causality. Residual limitations: savings is an assumed proxy for an unmeasured discounting trait; no 1981 time-preference measure (reverse/stable-trait signal in R10); non-random attrition by 1992 (30% weight missingness) and 31% income non-response; null effects for men and for BMI growth. For context, this aligns with the economic literature on impatience/time discounting and obesity.

payload.hypothesis: YES - higher time preference (proxied by taking money out of or not holding savings in 1989) is associated with higher BMI in 1992: +0.54 BMI units [0.15, 0.94] after full confounder adjustment.
payload.workflow: 1) Feature engineering: decoded Height1981 (ft*100+in), computed BMI=703*lb/in^2 with weight validated as pounds and height as inches (H1985 with H1981 fallback); 2) Time-preference proxy from savings direction 1989 (+ net savings amounts); 3) Primary OLS BMI1992 on TP with 16 confounders (age, sex, race/ethnicity, family size, parents' education, own education, ASVAB, income 1979/85/89, wealth 1985/90, incarceration), cluster SE by Sample ID; 4) 11 robustness checks (alternate proxy definitions, BMI1989, BMI change, implausible-BMI exclusion, median-imputation/missing flags, sex subgroups, occupation-at-14, wealth-accum proxy, reverse-temporal BMI1981).
